Yes, plants can survive without soil. According to multiple sources, soil itself is not strictly necessary for plant growth; what plants truly need are the functions soil provides—support, nutrients, moisture, and oxygen around the roots [d1]. As one source explains, "soil simply holds mineral nutrients close to plant roots, but the soil itself isn't necessary for plant growth" [d3]. The most well-known soil-free growing method is hydroponics, in which plants grow in nutrient-rich water; as confirmed by a science education resource, "Plants can survive without being planted in soil. The science of growing plants in nutrient-rich water is hydroponics" [d7]. Beyond hydroponics, aeroponics (roots suspended in air in a greenhouse) and water-only growing are also viable methods [d1]. Specific plants that naturally thrive without soil include orchids and air plants (Tillandsias), which absorb water and nutrients directly from the atmosphere [d2], as well as lucky bamboo, philodendron, and aloe vera, which can be grown in water or pebble-and-sand mixtures [d4][d8]. Even succulents, which generally need a potting medium, can survive up to about two weeks without soil in open air with proper care [d9].
